meta.title: Signal vs accretion — how much is early, how much was added
meta.note: A story is not written once; it grows. This is the mainstream philological picture of what is EARLY-ATTESTED (the recoverable core) versus what most scholars regard as LATER ACCRETION, and what is simply UNKNOWABLE. It is a map of scholarly confidence, not a verdict on truth — and the tradition holds a different view (single sage-authors), shown elsewhere and not blurred here. Datings are ranges; reasonable scholars disagree at the edges.

confidenceScale.label: Early core
confidenceScale.hint: The oldest recoverable layer — attested early, structurally central.

confidenceScale.label: Grew with the text
confidenceScale.hint: Part of the epic as it expanded; neither the oldest core nor a clearly late graft.

confidenceScale.label: Later addition
confidenceScale.hint: Widely regarded by scholars as added after the core — framing books, didactic sections, appendices.

confidenceScale.label: Regional / devotional accretion
confidenceScale.hint: Added in specific retellings or traditions, centuries later.

confidenceScale.label: Unknowable
confidenceScale.hint: The evidence does not let us say. We mark the gap rather than fill it.

layers.name: Books II–VI (Ayodhyā → Yuddha)
layers.what: The narrative core — exile, abduction, the search, the war. The oldest recoverable Rāmāyaṇa; Rāma here is a human hero, not yet fully divine.
layers.why: Structurally central, internally consistent, and the layer most free of the theological framing that Books I & VII add.
layers.source: Brockington, The Sanskrit Epics (1998); Goldman (gen. ed.), The Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, intro vols.

layers.name: Book I — Bāla Kāṇḍa
layers.what: Rāma's birth and childhood, and the framing that presents him as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.
layers.why: Widely regarded as a later addition: it carries the strongest divinity/theology, and sits awkwardly with the more human Rāma of the core.

layers.name: Book VII — Uttara Kāṇḍa
layers.what: The aftermath — Sītā's banishment, Lava & Kuśa, Rāma's end; much of Rāvaṇa's backstory.
layers.why: Also widely held to be a later addition; several of its most-discussed episodes (Sītā's second exile) are absent from, or contradict, the core's ending.

layers.name: Regional retellings' additions
layers.what: Episodes and figures added in later regional versions — e.g. the clown-god Semar and sons in the Javanese Kakawin, or the palace-politics emphasis of the Thai Ramakien.
layers.why: Absent from Vālmīki; introduced centuries later in specific cultures as the story was retold.
layers.source: Comparative studies of the Southeast-Asian Rāmāyaṇas.

layers.name: The ‘Jaya’ / Bhārata core
layers.what: The kernel — the Kuru succession dispute, the dice game, exile, and the 18-day war. Tradition itself remembers a shorter earlier text (‘Jaya’, then ‘Bhārata’) that grew into the Mahābhārata.
layers.why: The narrative spine around which everything else accretes; the epic's own frame verses distinguish it from the fuller text.

layers.name: Didactic parvans (Śānti, Anuśāsana)
layers.what: The vast teaching sections after the war — Bhīṣma's discourses on law, duty and liberation. Roughly a third of the whole text.
layers.why: Long recognised as a major later expansion: they halt the narrative for didactic material and swell the count toward 100,000 verses.

layers.name: Bhagavad Gītā
layers.what: Kṛṣṇa's teaching to Arjuna on the eve of battle (Bhīṣma Parva) — later read as a standalone scripture.
layers.why: Part of the epic's growth; scholars debate whether it is original to the battle scene or an early insertion, so we mark it 'grew' rather than 'core' or clearly 'added'.
layers.source: Brockington (1998); debate summarised in Gītā scholarship.

layers.name: Harivaṃśa (appendix)
layers.what: The ‘genealogy of Hari’ — Kṛṣṇa's life and lineage, appended as a khila (supplement) to the epic.
layers.why: Explicitly a supplement (khila), not one of the 18 parvans; a clear later attachment.
layers.source: Standard Mahābhārata textual histories; BORI critical edition.

layers.name: Frame stories & Purāṇic matter
layers.what: Nested frame-narrators (Ugraśravas → Śaunaka; Vaiśampāyana → Janamejaya), origin myths, tīrtha (pilgrimage) lists and genealogies woven throughout.
layers.why: The layered frames and encyclopaedic matter are widely read as accretions that turned a war-epic into a ‘complete’ compendium (‘what is here is everywhere…’).
